source.title: Curiously Effective Features For Image Quality Prediction
source.authors: Sören Becker; T. Wiegand; S. Bosse

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no truncation or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: It measures performance while varying the number of selected features in several feature-regression models, using a different setup from the original deep-network studies.
record.gate_note: The feature-count sweep in Fig. 2 is the result bearing on the versions tested. Tables 1 and 2 compare quality-prediction performance across codebooks and datasets but do not sweep model capacity; spectral analyses do not measure the claimed curve. Results from cited work are not treated as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps the number of input features to a linear SVR on LIVE image-quality data for five codebooks. Its own Fig. 2 shows correlation rising, dipping near the stated interpolation point (~605 training samples), then rising to a maximum in the overparameterized regime. This is a new setting and model class for the capacity-wise double-descent curve, so it bears on V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors find that random-noise or patch codebooks give quality-prediction correlations on par with learned CORNIA codes. They find that performance depends critically on feature count, with peaks in the highly overparameterized regime, which they liken to double descent. They conclude that many feature extractors can compensate for, or outperform, fewer individually better ones.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a CORNIA-inspired shallow feature model and SVR, and varies selected feature count while measuring MOS correlation; it is not the original deep-network size, epoch, or sample-size setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The curve is reported for the LIVE database and varies with selected feature count; this sweep is not reported for the TID2013 or CSIQ cross-database evaluations.
record.peer_reviewed: To appear in Proc. ICIP 2021, as stated in the paper text.
record.problems: The curve is shown only in a figure, without numerical values or reported error bars. The authors note that the study uses a single computational model; the feature-count sweep is reported on LIVE.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for Tables 1 and 2: those report codebook and cross-database performance comparisons, not the feature-count curve relevant to V4.

untested.parts: No deep networks. The model is a shallow codebook plus linear SVR, and the depth is not varied.
There is no sweep over training epochs or training time.
The number of training samples is not varied.
No effective-complexity measure is tested across size, epoch and sample axes. Only the raw count of SVR parameters versus samples (~605) is mentioned.
Label noise and regularization strength are not varied (fixed default NuSVR C=1). Multiple peaks are not examined.
The curve is not re-expressed against an alternative effective-parameter count.

record.verdict_notes:
Caveats on the V4 support:
- The measure is Pearson correlation with MOS (higher is better), not test risk, so the 'descent' appears as a dip in correlation.
- Features are added in order of their importance (absolute SVR coefficients) in a model trained on all features over the same splits. This is a data-dependent ordering, not a standard capacity sweep.
- The dip's position relative to ~605 is asserted in the text, not quantified. No numbers or error bars are given.
- The sweep is reported only on LIVE. Tables 1–2 (fixed full-feature performance across codebooks and databases) correctly have no rows.
- At small feature counts CORNIA outperforms the random codebooks. Differences become negligible at 2000 or more features.
- Tranche changed from the reader's T2 to T3: this is a new application setting rather than a different method aimed at the original question.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test model-wise double descent in deep networks; the evaluated framework is a shallow feature model with SVR.
No training-sample-size sweep near an interpolation threshold.
Tests feature-count curves for five codebook models on LIVE; does not test every model class or risk measure.

Reports a feature-count sweep and an approximate interpolation-point parameter count, but does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and samples.
Does not vary label noise or regularization, or test triple/multiple descent.
Does not compare the curve with an alternative effective-parameter count or show that such a count makes it an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.note: The text says performance across models first rises, descends, then rises and saturates; CORNIA is one of the plotted model curves. The authors place the interpolation point at approximately 605 learned SVR parameters.
